Differential salivary disposition of linezolid and its two major metabolites (PNU-142300 and PNU-142586) after a single dose in healthy adults

Metadata and scope

AuthorsYasuhiro Tsuji; Hitoshi Kawasuji; Tomona Yamada; Fumihiro Kurosaki; Naoki Oikawa; Makito Kaneda; Takahiko Aoyama; Taketo Uchiyama; Yoshihiro Yamamoto
SourceJournal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy. 2026;81:dkag280.
IdentifierDOI: 10.1093/jac/dkag280
DesignExploratory single-dose pharmacokinetic study using stored samples from a prior study; six healthy adult male volunteers.
InterventionLinezolid 600 mg IV over 1 hour.
Sampling12 serum + 15 saliva samples per participant over 0–10 h.
Scope warning. This is a six-participant, single-dose healthy-volunteer study. It does not validate salivary TDM at steady state, in patients with renal impairment, in women, or for clinical outcomes such as thrombocytopenia.

One-page synthesis

Core thesis: after a single 600 mg IV dose, salivary linezolid closely tracked protein-unbound serum exposure, while PNU-142300 and PNU-142586 remained below the assay quantification limit in every saliva sample despite measurable serum exposure.

The most clinically useful numerical comparison is the parent-drug exposure: mean salivary linezolid AUC0–∞ was 191.80 µg·h/mL versus 184.10 µg·h/mL for serum-unbound linezolid, a reported mean ratio of approximately 1.04. Salivary Cmax was 17.46 µg/mL versus 14.28 µg/mL unbound in serum. In contrast, both metabolites were quantifiable in total and unbound serum but were BLQ in saliva at every time point for every participant.

The metabolite protein-binding estimates are less secure than the linezolid saliva finding. Mean PB was 7.02% for PNU-142300 and 8.69% for PNU-142586, but PNU-142300's unbound AUC0–∞ slightly exceeded total AUC and PNU-142586 PB showed large interindividual variability. The authors therefore caution that the ultrafiltration method could not precisely characterize metabolite protein binding. The study supports saliva as a research matrix for parent linezolid under the tested conditions, but it does not establish a clinically interchangeable salivary TDM strategy.

Best-supported finding: parent linezolid was consistently measurable in saliva with exposure similar to protein-unbound serum over the studied single-dose period.
Do not overclaim: “BLQ in saliva” is not proof that metabolites can never be monitored in saliva. The study's assay sensitivity, single-dose exposure, and small healthy cohort limit that conclusion.

Section condensation

Introduction

The rationale combines two observations: linezolid TDM is clinically important because exposure relates to thrombocytopenia, and its two major metabolites may accumulate disproportionately with renal impairment. Prior work suggested saliva can track linezolid, but the protein binding and salivary disposition of PNU-142300 and PNU-142586 had not been characterized. The study therefore asked whether these metabolites are quantifiable in saliva and how their serum and salivary PK compare with the parent drug.

Methods and experiments

Stored samples from a previous study were reanalyzed. Six healthy adult men (mean age 31 years; mean weight 67.0 kg) received linezolid 600 mg IV over 1 hour. Each contributed 12 serum and 15 saliva samples from 0 to 10 hours. Total and protein-unbound serum concentrations and saliva concentrations of linezolid, PNU-142300, and PNU-142586 were quantified by HPLC. Serum unbound fractions were obtained by ultrafiltration; saliva was analyzed without ultrafiltration. LLOQ was 0.1 µg/mL for linezolid and PNU-142300 and 0.2 µg/mL for PNU-142586.

Noncompartmental analysis calculated Cmax, Tmax, AUC0–10, AUC0–∞, and protein binding. AUC0–∞ was extrapolated from the last quantifiable concentration and terminal elimination rate. PB was computed from paired total and unbound concentrations at Cmax. The analysis used R 4.3.2 and reported package versions.

Results

Linezolid was quantifiable in all matrices. Its saliva time course visually resembled serum-unbound exposure, with mean salivary Cmax 17.46 µg/mL and AUC0–∞ 191.80 µg·h/mL compared with unbound serum Cmax 14.28 µg/mL and AUC0–∞ 184.10 µg·h/mL. The study reports a saliva-to-unbound-serum mean AUC0–∞ ratio of approximately 1.04.

Both metabolites were readily measurable in serum. For PNU-142300, total/unbound AUC0–∞ was 10.97/11.05 µg·h/mL; for PNU-142586 it was 18.00/15.28 µg·h/mL. Yet all saliva measurements for both metabolites were BLQ. Mean PB estimates were 7.02% for PNU-142300 and 8.69% for PNU-142586, with the latter showing substantial variability.

Discussion

The authors interpret the parent-drug data as consistent with saliva reflecting the protein-unbound fraction of linezolid. They are more cautious about the metabolite PB estimates because PNU-142300 had an unbound-to-total AUC ratio slightly above 1 and PNU-142586 PB varied widely; small adsorption effects during ultrafiltration were inconsistent and were not corrected. An additional ADMET Predictor analysis suggested that the metabolites are predominantly ionized at salivary and blood pH, unlike predominantly molecular linezolid, offering a mechanistic hypothesis for poorer salivary transfer.

The discussion explicitly limits clinical extrapolation. Single-dose exposure in six healthy men may not resemble steady-state concentrations or accumulation in renal impairment. Because both metabolites were BLQ in saliva, saliva-to-serum ratios could not be estimated, and an effect of analytical sensitivity cannot be excluded. The 0–10 h period did not adequately characterize the terminal metabolite phase; salivary pH and flow were not systematically assessed; and no women were enrolled.

Conclusions

The authors conclude that salivary linezolid concentrations closely reflected serum-unbound exposure after a single IV dose in healthy adults. PNU-142300 and PNU-142586 remained BLQ in saliva despite measurable serum exposure, so blood-based measurements were required for metabolite exposure assessment under these assay and study conditions. They frame salivary linezolid monitoring as worthy of further evaluation rather than established practice.

PK calculation workflow

Inputs: serial serum total, serum unbound, and saliva concentrations over 0–10 h.
Cmax: highest observed concentration.
Tmax: elapsed time from infusion start.
AUC0–10: trapezoidal rule.
ke: log-linear regression in the terminal phase.
AUC0–∞ = AUC0–10 + Ct / ke, where Ct is the last quantifiable concentration ≤10 h.
Protein binding (%) = ([total − unbound] / total) × 100 at each participant's Cmax.
Failure mode noted by source: terminal metabolite elimination was not adequately characterized over 0–10 h, and metabolite ultrafiltration estimates were imprecise.

Evaluation and appraisal

Verdict: Read soon. The paper is a focused, useful PK methods study for linezolid TDM research, but it should not be used by itself to change clinical monitoring practice.
8/10
Relevance

Directly relevant to linezolid TDM and non-invasive PK sampling.

Evidence basis: Paired serum total/unbound and saliva measurements address a practical monitoring question.
Limiting factor: Only a six-person healthy-volunteer single-dose study.
Would raise/lower: Clinical steady-state validation with trough/AUC targets and outcomes would raise this score.

7/10
Novelty

Adds direct characterization of salivary disposition for both major linezolid metabolites.

Evidence basis: The metabolite saliva findings and paired protein-unbound serum measurements address a stated evidence gap.
Limiting factor: The parent-linezolid saliva concept was already established in prior work.
Would raise/lower: Replication in patients and mechanistic validation would increase novelty/impact.

5/10
Method strength

Careful serial paired sampling and HPLC quantification are offset by a very small, narrow cohort and method limitations.

Evidence basis: Twelve serum and 15 saliva samples per participant, explicit LLOQs, ultrafiltration, and noncompartmental analysis.
Limiting factor: n=6, all male, stored-sample reanalysis, and imprecise metabolite protein-binding estimation.
Would raise/lower: Larger prospective sampling with validated unbound-metabolite methods would raise the score.

5/10
Evidence strength

The study directly supports the in-study BLQ and parent-linezolid exposure observations, but not broader clinical TDM claims.

Evidence basis: All metabolite saliva samples were BLQ; linezolid saliva AUC0–∞ approximated serum-unbound AUC0–∞.
Limiting factor: No confidence intervals, tiny sample, limited terminal phase, and analytical sensitivity may influence BLQ findings.
Would raise/lower: Patient replication with a more sensitive assay and prespecified agreement criteria would raise the score.

2/10
External validity

Generalizability is poor beyond the exact experimental setting.

Evidence basis: Participants were healthy adult men receiving one IV dose.
Limiting factor: No women, patients, renal impairment, repeated dosing, steady state, oral dosing, or clinical outcomes.
Would raise/lower: A diverse clinical cohort across renal function and steady state would materially raise the score.

4/10
Implementation value

Useful for designing future salivary linezolid studies, but insufficient to change routine TDM practice.

Evidence basis: Provides sampling, assay, LLOQ, and PK benchmarks and shows current saliva assay failure for the metabolites.
Limiting factor: No validation against clinical targets or toxicity, and metabolite saliva exposure was unmeasurable.
Would raise/lower: Demonstrated accuracy for clinically relevant trough/AUC targets and outcome-linked thresholds would raise the score.

Main strengths

  • Paired total serum, unbound serum, and saliva measurements in the same participants.
  • Dense serial sampling over the first 10 hours and explicit assay LLOQs.
  • Direct visualization of individual trajectories rather than only pooled summaries.
  • Transparent reporting of ultrafiltration anomalies and reasons not to overinterpret metabolite protein binding.
  • The discussion generally respects the boundary between the observed single-dose data and clinical steady-state questions.

Main limitations

  • Very small and narrow cohort: six healthy men, no women, no infected patients, and no renal impairment.
  • Single-dose design: cannot establish steady-state saliva-serum relationships or metabolite accumulation.
  • Short terminal window: the source itself states that metabolite terminal elimination was insufficiently characterized during 0–10 h.
  • BLQ ambiguity: all metabolite saliva samples were below assay sensitivity, preventing estimation of saliva-to-serum ratios and leaving open whether a more sensitive assay or higher steady-state exposure would detect them.
  • Protein-binding uncertainty: PNU-142300 unbound exposure slightly exceeded total exposure and PNU-142586 PB was highly variable, indicating limited precision of the ultrafiltration method.
  • No clinical validation: no agreement thresholds, trough prediction, toxicity endpoints, or decision-impact analysis.
Practice boundary: do not infer that salivary linezolid can replace blood-based TDM in routine patients, or that saliva can never quantify the metabolites. The study only establishes what occurred with this dose, cohort, sampling window, and assay.

Implementation / practice takeaways

Use nowUse the paper as methodological evidence that salivary linezolid can approximate unbound serum exposure in a controlled single-dose setting.
Do not use nowDo not substitute saliva for serum in routine linezolid TDM solely on this study, and do not rely on saliva for PNU-142300/PNU-142586 with the reported assay.
Best next studyProspective steady-state paired sampling in clinical patients across renal function, including women, with a more sensitive metabolite assay and standardized salivary pH/flow measurement.
Clinically meaningful validationTest agreement for Cmin/AUC targets and association with thrombocytopenia or other relevant outcomes rather than only concentration correlation.
